doc.title: Ellen Rowe interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 2, 2024

title: Charts without improvised solos
summary: Rowe has never written a chart with no solos; they matter for players, students and the length of a piece.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Have you ever written a chart that did not have any improvised solos in it?

I haven’t, and I’ve thought a lot about Brookmeyer and Bill Holman says this too sometimes in that — I can’t remember which one of them it was who was saying this but hey this is my music, I want control over it, I don’t think there is the need constantly to always have improvised solos. But you know I’m generally writing for bands where it’s expected to have improvised solos and there’s great soloists, or I’m writing secondary school music and you want the students improvising. It’s critical, you know, part of their — so I haven’t really been in a situation — maybe I wrote one piece where there is this very short amount of improvisation but in general I haven’t done that.

It’s tricky because I’ve tried it one or two times and what you find is you’re writing and writing and writing and then you come up — so far I’ve got 90 seconds of music. You know we rely on improvised solos to at least give some length to the piece.

We do, yeah. And frankly it’s a moment where I know the rhythm section is just like oh thank God, I can just comp, I can just walk, I can whatever. And I know my band, my University of Michigan band, that’s a moment where they kind of come together and they look at the soloists and they’re really enjoying what the soloist is doing. And it’s a feel good moment, so obviously there’s a lot of benefits to it, but yeah. It would be hard to do that.
